results.question: What exactly is culpable homicide under the new Indian criminal law?
results.ground_truth: 100. Whoever causes death by doing an act with the intention of causing death, or with the intention of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, or with the knowledge that he is likely by such act to cause death, commits the offence of culpable homicide.
results.answer: Culpable homicide under the new Indian criminal law, as specified in Section 101 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), is defined as the act of causing death in circumstances where: (a) the act is done with the intention to cause death; or (b) with the intention of causing such bodily injury as the offender knows is likely to cause death; or (c) with the intention of causing bodily injury, and the injury is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death; or (d) the offender knows that the act is so imminently dangerous that it must, in all probability, cause death or bodily injury likely to cause death, and does so without excuse for incurring such risk. These are the general conditions under which an act causing death is treated as culpable homicide under the BNS, unless specifically excepted.

results.question: What is the punishment for murder in India under the new law?
results.ground_truth: 103. (1) Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine. (2) When a group of five or more persons acting in concert commits murder on the ground of race, caste or community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief or any other similar ground each member of such group shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.
results.answer: The punishment for murder in India under the new law is death or imprisonment for life, and the offender shall also be liable to fine [BNS | active | substantive | Section 103].

results.question: What does 'rape' mean legally under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita?
results.ground_truth: 63. A man is said to commit "rape" if he—(a) penetrates his penis, to any extent, into the vagina, mouth, urethra or anus of a woman or makes her to do so with him or any other person; or (b) inserts, to any extent, any object or a part of the body, not being the penis, into the vagina, the urethra or anus of a woman or makes her to do so with him or any other person; or (c) manipulates any part of the body of a woman so as to cause penetration into the vagina, urethra, anus or any part of body of such woman or makes her to do so with him or any other person; or (d) applies his mouth to the vagina, anus, urethra of a woman or makes her to do so with him or any other person, under the circumstances falling under any of the following seven descriptions:—(i) against her will; (ii) without her consent; (iii) with her consent, when her consent has been obtained by putting her or any person in whom she is interested, in fear of death or of hurt; (iv) with her consent, when the man knows that he is not her husband and that her consent is given because she believes that he is another man to whom she is or believes herself to be lawfully married; (v) with her consent when, at the time of giving such consent, by reason of unsoundness of mind or intoxication or the administration by him personally or through another of any stupefying or unwholesome substance, she is unable to understand the nature and consequences of that to which she gives consent; (vi) with or without her consent, when she is under eighteen years of age; (vii) when she is unable to communicate consent.
results.answer: Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, a man is said to commit 'rape' if he performs any of the following acts: (a) penetrates his penis, to any extent, into the vagina, mouth, urethra or anus of a woman or makes her do so with him or any other person; (b) inserts, to any extent, any object or part of the body, not being the penis, into the vagina, urethra or anus of a woman or makes her do so with him or any other person; (c) manipulates any part of the body of a woman to cause penetration into the vagina, urethra, anus or any part of the body of such woman or makes her do so with him or any other person; or (d) applies his mouth to the vagina, anus, urethra of a woman or makes her to do so with him or any other person, under certain circumstances such as against her will, without her consent, or with consent obtained by threat, among others. The complete legal definition includes several more detailed criteria and circumstances wherein these acts amount to rape.

results.question: What is robbery and how is it defined in the BNS?
results.ground_truth: 309. (1) In all robbery there is either theft or extortion. (2) Theft is robbery if, in order to the committing of the theft, or in committing the theft, or in carrying away or attempting to carry away property obtained by the theft, the offender, for that end voluntarily causes or attempts to cause to any person death or hurt or wrongful restraint, or fear of instant death or of instant hurt, or of instant wrongful restraint. (3) Extortion is robbery if the offender, at the time of committing the extortion, is in the presence of the person put in fear, and commits the extortion by putting that person in fear of instant death, of instant hurt, or of instant wrongful restraint to that person or to some other person, and, by so putting in fear, induces the person so put in fear then and there to deliver up the thing extorted.
results.answer: Robbery is defined in the BNS as an offence in which there is either theft or extortion. Theft becomes robbery if, in order to commit the theft, while committing it, or while carrying away or attempting to carry away the property obtained by the theft, the offender voluntarily causes or attempts to cause to any person death, hurt, wrongful restraint, or fear of instant death, instant hurt, or instant wrongful restraint [BNS | active | substantive | Section 309].

results.question: What does 'grievous hurt' mean under Indian law?
results.ground_truth: 116. The following kinds of hurt only are designated as "grievous", namely:—(a) Emasculation; (b) Permanent privation of the sight of either eye; (c) Permanent privation of the hearing of either ear; (d) Privation of any member or joint; (e) Destruction or permanent impairing of the powers of any member or joint; (f) Permanent disfiguration of the head or face; (g) Fracture or dislocation of a bone or tooth; (h) Any hurt which endangers life or which causes the sufferer to be during the space of fifteen days in severe bodily pain, or unable to follow his ordinary pursuits.
results.answer: Under Indian law, 'grievous hurt' refers to harm that is severe and grave in nature. According to Section 117 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), a person is said to voluntarily cause grievous hurt if they intend to cause or know themselves likely to cause grievous hurt, and actually cause such grievous hurt to another. Thus, 'grievous hurt' involves not just causing harm, but harm of a particularly serious nature, distinguished from ordinary hurt by both the intent and the resulting severity of injury [BNS | active | substantive | Section 117].

(1) Whoever does any act with the intent to threaten or likely to threaten the unity, integrity, sovereignty, security, or economic security of India or with the intent to strike terror or likely to strike terror in the people or any section of the people in India or in any foreign country,—(a) by using bombs, dynamite or other explosive substance or inflammable substance or firearms or other lethal weapons or poisonous or noxious gases or other chemicals or by any other substance (whether biological, radioactive, nuclear or otherwise) of a hazardous nature or by any other means of whatever nature to cause or likely to cause—(i) death of, or injury to, any person or persons; or (ii) loss of, or damage to, or destruction of, property; or (iii) disruption of any supplies or services essential to the life of the community in India or in any foreign country; or (iv) damage to, the monetary stability of India by way of production or smuggling or circulation of counterfeit Indian paper currency, coin or of any other material; or (v) damage or destruction of any property in India or in a foreign country used or intended to be used for the defence of India or in connection with any other purposes of the Government of India, any State Government or any of their agencies; or (b) overawes by means of criminal force or the show of criminal force or attempts to do so or causes death of any public functionary or attempts to cause death of any public functionary; or (c) detains, kidnaps or abducts any person and threatening to kill or injure such person or does any other act in order to compel the Government of India, any State Government or the Government of a foreign country or an international or inter-governmental organisation or any other person to do or abstain from doing any act, commit a terrorist act.
results.answer: A 'terrorist act' as defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita is an act committed with the intent to threaten or likely to threaten the unity, integrity, sovereignty, security, or economic security of India, or with the intent to strike terror or likely to strike terror in the people or any section of the people in India or in any foreign country. This can include acts using bombs, dynamite, explosives, inflammable substances, firearms, lethal weapons, poisonous or noxious gases, chemicals, or any other hazardous substances, whether biological, radioactive, nuclear, or otherwise, or by any other means of whatever nature to cause or likely to cause such threats or terror.

results.question: What is cruelty to a wife under the new law and what is the punishment?
results.ground_truth: 85. Whoever, being the husband or the relative of the husband of a woman, subjects such woman to cruelty shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine. 86. results.question: When can a person use deadly force in self-defence under the new law?
results.ground_truth: 38. The right of private defence of the body extends, under the restrictions specified in section 37, to the voluntary causing of death or of any other harm to the assailant, if the offence which occasions the exercise of the right be of any of the descriptions hereinafter enumerated, namely:—(a) such an assault as may reasonably cause the apprehension that death will otherwise be the consequence of such assault; (b) such an assault as may reasonably cause the apprehension that grievous hurt will otherwise be the consequence of such assault; (c) an assault with the intention of committing rape; (d) an assault with the intention of gratifying unnatural lust; (e) an assault with the intention of kidnapping or abducting; (f) an assault with the intention of wrongfully confining a person, under circumstances which may reasonably cause him to apprehend that he will be unable to have recourse to the public authorities for his release; (g) an act of throwing or administering acid or an attempt to throw or administer acid which may reasonably cause the apprehension that grievous hurt will otherwise be the consequence of such act.
results.answer: A person can use deadly force in self-defence under the new law when exercising the right of private defence of the body against certain types of offences. Specifically, the right of private defence extends to causing death or any other harm to the assailant if the assault creates a reasonable apprehension that death or grievous hurt will otherwise be the consequence, or if the assault is committed with the intention of committing rape, gratifying unnatural lust, kidnapping, or abducting. However, these rights are subject to the restrictions specified in Section 37 [BNS | active | substantive | Section 38].

results.question: What is the offence of 'act endangering sovereignty and integrity of India' in the new law — and how does it differ from the old sedition law?
results.ground_truth: [IPC Section 124A — Sedition:] Whoever, by words, either spoken or written, or by signs, or by visible representation, or otherwise, brings or attempts to bring into hatred or contempt, or excites or attempts to excite disaffection towards, the Government established by law in India, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, to which fine may be added, or with imprisonment which may extend to three years, to which fine may be added, or with fine. Explanation 1.—The expression "disaffection" includes disloyalty and all feelings of enmity. Explanation 2.—Comments expressing disapprobation of the measures of the Government with a view to obtain their alteration by lawful means without exciting or attempting to excite any feelings of disaffection, do not constitute an offence under this section. [BNS Section 152:] Whoever, purposely or knowingly, by words, either spoken or written, or by signs, or by visible representation, or by electronic communication or by use of financial mean, or otherwise, excites or attempts to excite, secession or armed rebellion or subversive activities, or encourages feelings of separatist activities or endangers sovereignty or unity and integrity of India; or indulges in or commits any such act shall be punished with imprisonment for life or with imprisonment which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine. Explanation.—Comments expressing disapprobation of the measures, or administrative or other action of the Government with a view to obtain their alteration by lawful means without exciting or attempting to excite the activities referred to in this section do not constitute an offence under this section.

results.question: What is 'petty organised crime' under the new Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita?
results.ground_truth: 112. (1) Whoever, being a member of a group or gang, either singly or jointly, commits any act of theft, snatching, cheating, unauthorised selling of tickets, unauthorised betting or gambling, selling of public examination question papers or any other similar criminal act, is said to commit petty organised crime. Explanation.—For the purposes of this sub-section "theft" includes trick theft, theft from vehicle, dwelling house or business premises, cargo theft, pick pocketing, theft through card skimming, shoplifting and theft of Automated Teller Machine. (2) Whoever commits any petty organised crime shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than one year but which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

results.question: If someone kills another during grave and sudden provocation, is it still murder?
results.ground_truth: Exception 1.—Culpable homicide is not murder if the offender, whilst deprived of the power of self-control by grave and sudden provocation, causes the death of the person who gave the provocation or causes the death of any other person by mistake or accident: Provided that the provocation is not,—(a) sought or voluntarily provoked by the offender as an excuse for killing or doing harm to any person; (b) given by anything done in obedience to the law, or by a public servant in the lawful exercise of the powers of such public servant; (c) given by anything done in the lawful exercise of the right of private defence. Explanation.—Whether the provocation was grave and sudden enough to prevent the offence from amounting to murder is a question of fact.

results.question: Is BNS community service an entirely new punishment that didn't exist before?
results.ground_truth: [IPC Section 53 — Punishments:] The punishments to which offenders are liable under the provisions of this Code are—First.—Death; Secondly.—Imprisonment for life; Thirdly.—[Omitted]; Fourthly.—Imprisonment, which is of two descriptions, namely:—(1) Rigorous, that is, with hard labour; (2) Simple; Fifthly.—Forfeiture of property; Sixthly.—Fine. [BNS Section 4 — Punishments:] The punishments to which offenders are liable under the provisions of this Sanhita are—(a) Death; (b) Imprisonment for life; (c) Imprisonment, which is of two descriptions, namely:—(1) Rigorous, that is, with hard labour; (2) Simple; (d) Forfeiture of property; (e) Fine; (f) Community Service. [Community Service is thus a new addition in BNS not present in IPC Section 53.]
results.answer: Community service as a form of punishment is explicitly provided for under the BNS (Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023). According to the provided context, it allows the court to order a convict to perform work that benefits the community, for which the convict is not entitled to remuneration [BNSS | active | procedural | Section 23]. This form of punishment is also mentioned as an option for offenses such as failing to appear in response to a proclamation [BNS | active | substantive | Section 209]. In contrast, the repealed IPC sections provided do not mention community service as a form of punishment (they only mention imprisonment, fine, etc.) [IPC | repealed | substantive | Section 53]. Therefore, BNS community service constitutes a new, explicit statutory form of punishment that was not specified under the IPC.

results.question: After how many days can a Magistrate take cognizance and what is the process?
results.ground_truth: 210. (1) Subject to the provisions of this Chapter, any Magistrate of the first class, and any Magistrate of the second class specially empowered in this behalf under sub-section (2), may take cognizance of any offence—(a) upon receiving a complaint of facts, including any complaint filed by a person authorised under any special law, which constitutes such offence; (b) upon a police report (submitted in any mode including electronic mode) of such facts; (c) upon information received from any person other than a police officer, or upon his own knowledge, that such offence has been committed.
results.answer:
The provided context does not specify any fixed number of days after which a Magistrate can take cognizance of an offence. Rather, it details the process through which a Magistrate may take cognizance and proceed with a case. 

Specifically, if a complaint is made to a Magistrate under Section 379 or 380, the Magistrate shall proceed to deal with the case as if it were instituted on a police report, notwithstanding anything contained in Chapter XVI [BNSS | active | procedural | Section 382]. Furthermore, if there is a related appeal pending, the Magistrate may adjourn the case until the appeal is decided [BNSS | active | procedural | Section 382].

If a complaint is made to a Magistrate who is not competent to take cognizance of the offence, the complaint must be returned for presentation to the proper court if it is in writing, or the complainant is directed to the proper court if the complaint is not in writing [BNSS | active | procedural | Section 224].

Therefore, the process involves determining the competence of the Magistrate and, if competent, proceeding with the complaint or police report. There is no mention of a specific number of days for taking cognizance in the given context.

results.question: Is a confession made to a police officer admissible as evidence in India?
results.ground_truth: 23. (1) No confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence. (2) No confession made by any person while he is in the custody of a police officer, unless it is made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate shall be proved against him: Provided that when any fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of information received from a person accused of any offence, in the custody of a police officer, so much of such information, whether it amounts to a confession or not, as relates distinctly to the fact discovered, may be proved.
results.answer: No, a confession made to a police officer is not admissible as evidence against a person accused of any offence in India. Additionally, a confession made by any person while in the custody of a police officer cannot be proved against him unless it is made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate. However, if a fact is discovered as a consequence of information received from an accused person in custody, so much of that information as relates distinctly to the fact discovered may be proved [BSA | active | evidentiary | Section 23].

results.question: What is a 'dying declaration' and is it admissible as evidence even without cross-examination?
results.ground_truth: 26. Statements, written or verbal, of relevant facts made by a person who is dead, or who cannot be found, or who has become incapable of giving evidence, or whose attendance cannot be procured without an amount of delay or expense which under the circumstances of the case appears to the Court unreasonable, are themselves relevant facts in the following cases, namely:—(a) when the statement is made by a person as to the cause of his death, or as to any of the circumstances of the transaction which resulted in his death, in cases in which the cause of that person's death comes into question. Such statements are relevant whether the person who made them was or was not, at the time when they were made, under expectation of death, and whatever may be the nature of the proceeding in which the cause of his death comes into question.
results.answer: A 'dying declaration' refers to a statement made by a person about the cause of their death or the circumstances which resulted in their death, made when the person believes death is imminent. The admissibility of a dying declaration as evidence generally does not require cross-examination. However, in the context of the provided material, it is specifically illustrated that if someone wishes to prove a dying declaration, they must first prove the death of the person who made the declaration. This is a condition precedent for the admissibility of the dying declaration as evidence [BSA | active | evidentiary | Section 107]. results.question: How is a confession obtained by threat or coercion treated under Indian evidence law?
results.ground_truth: 22. A confession made by an accused person is irrelevant in a criminal proceeding, if the making of the confession appears to the Court to have been caused by any inducement, threat, coercion or promise having reference to the charge against the accused person, proceeding from a person in authority and sufficient, in the opinion of the Court, to give the accused person grounds which would appear to him reasonable for supposing that by making it he would gain any advantage or avoid any evil of a temporal nature in reference to the proceedings against him.
results.answer: A confession obtained by threat, inducement, coercion, or promise is considered irrelevant in a criminal proceeding if it appears to the Court that the confession was caused by such factors, especially if they reference the charge and come from a person in authority, and the accused might reasonably believe that making the confession would help him gain an advantage or avoid any temporal harm. However, if it appears to the Court that the influence of the threat, inducement, coercion, or promise was fully removed when the confession was made, the confession may be considered relevant. Also, such a confession does not become irrelevant merely because it was made under promise of secrecy or similar circumstances, provided other criteria of relevance are satisfied [BSA | active | evidentiary | Section 22].

results.ground_truth: 23. (1) No confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence. results.answer: The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) continues the position previously established under the Indian Evidence Act (IEA) regarding confessions to police. Both prohibit confessions made to a police officer from being proved against an accused person. Specifically, under BSA Section 23, no confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence, and no confession made by a person while in police custody shall be proved unless made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate [BSA | active | evidentiary | Section 23]. This is aligned with the repealed IEA, where Section 25 stated that confessions to police officers are not to be proved, and Section 26 provided that confessions made in police custody are not to be proved against the accused unless made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate [IEA | repealed | evidentiary | Section 25][IEA | repealed | evidentiary | Section 26]. Thus, the BSA essentially retains the same protections as the IEA regarding the inadmissibility of police confessions, without introducing substantial changes in substance.

results.question: What was the IPC definition of murder and how does it differ from the BNS?
results.ground_truth: [IPC Section 300:] Murder.—Except in the cases hereinafter excepted, culpable homicide is murder, if the act by which the death is caused is done with the intention of causing death, or—2ndly.—If it is done with the intention of causing such bodily injury as the offender knows to be likely to cause the death of the person to whom the harm is caused, or—3rdly.—If it is done with the intention of causing bodily injury to any person and the bodily injury intended to be inflicted is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, or—4thly.—If the person committing the act knows that it is so imminently dangerous that it must, in all probability, cause death, or such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, and commits such act without any excuse for incurring the risk of causing death or such injury as aforesaid. [BNS Section 101:] Except in the cases hereinafter excepted, culpable homicide is murder,—(a) if the act by which the death is caused is done with the intention of causing death; or (b) if the act by which the death is caused is done with the intention of causing such bodily injury as the offender knows to be likely to cause the death of the person to whom the harm is caused; or (c) if the act by which the death is caused is done with the intention of causing bodily injury to any person and the bodily injury intended to be inflicted is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death; or (d) if the person committing the act by which the death is caused, knows that it is so imminently dangerous that it must, in all probability, cause death, or such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, and commits such act without any excuse for incurring the risk of causing death or such injury as aforesaid.
results.answer: The IPC definition of murder is not explicitly provided in the context, as Section 300 IPC is only referenced by title and not by text. However, the BNS definition of murder, as provided, specifies that culpable homicide is murder except in certain cases, outlining specific circumstances (intention to cause death, knowledge of likely death, bodily injury sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature, or imminently dangerous act) under which an act qualifies as murder. The difference, based solely on the context, is that the new BNS Section 101 provides a detailed formulation for what constitutes murder, whereas the explicit definition from IPC Section 300 is not included in the context. Thus, based on the information given, only the BNS definition can be commented upon.

results.ground_truth: [IPC Section 375:] A man is said to commit "rape" who, except in the case hereinafter excepted, has sexual intercourse with a woman under circumstances falling under any of the six following descriptions:—First.—Against her will. Secondly.—Without her consent. Thirdly.—With her consent, when her consent has been obtained by putting her or any person in whom she is interested in fear of death or of hurt. Fourthly.—With her consent, when the man knows that he is not her husband, and that her consent is given because she believes that he is another man to whom she is or believes herself to be lawfully married. Fifthly.—With her consent, when, at the time of giving such consent, by reason of unsoundness of mind or intoxication or the administration by him personally or through another of any stupefying or unwholesome substance, she is unable to understand the nature and consequences of that to which she gives consent. Sixthly.—With or without her consent, when she is under sixteen years of age. Explanation.—Penetration is sufficient to constitute the sexual intercourse necessary to the offence of rape. Exception.—Sexual intercourse by a man with his own wife, the wife not being under fifteen years of age, is not rape. [BNS Section 63:] A man is said to commit "rape" if he—(a) penetrates his penis, to any extent, into the vagina, mouth, urethra or anus of a woman or makes her to do so with him or any other person; or (b) inserts, to any extent, any object or a part of the body, not being the penis, into the vagina, the urethra or anus of a woman or makes her to do so with him or any other person; or (c) manipulates any part of the body of a woman so as to cause penetration into the vagina, urethra, anus or any part of body of such woman or makes her to do so with him or any other person; or (d) applies his mouth to the vagina, anus, urethra of a woman or makes her to do so with him or any other person, under the circumstances falling under any of the following seven descriptions:—(i) against her will; (ii) without her consent; ...(vi) with or without her consent, when she is under eighteen years of age; (vii) when she is unable to communicate consent. Exception 2.—Sexual intercourse or sexual acts by a man with his own wife, the wife not being under eighteen years of age, is not rape. [Key differences: BNS expanded the physical acts constituting rape beyond penile-vaginal intercourse; raised age of consent from 16 to 18; raised marital rape exception from 15 to 18 years; added inability to communicate consent as a new circumstance.]

The provision lists out several specific situations in which the act constitutes rape [IPC | repealed | substantive | Section 375].

results.question: What was the IPC provision on sedition and how does it compare to the new BNS?
results.ground_truth: [IPC Section 124A — Sedition:] Whoever, by words, either spoken or written, or by signs, or by visible representation, or otherwise, brings or attempts to bring into hatred or contempt, or excites or attempts to excite disaffection towards, the Government established by law in India, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, to which fine may be added, or with imprisonment which may extend to three years, to which fine may be added, or with fine. Explanation 1.—The expression "disaffection" includes disloyalty and all feelings of enmity. Explanation 2.—Comments expressing disapprobation of the measures of the Government with a view to obtain their alteration by lawful means without exciting or attempting to excite any feelings of disaffection, do not constitute an offence under this section. [BNS Section 152 — Act endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India:] Whoever, purposely or knowingly, by words, either spoken or written, or by signs, or by visible representation, or by electronic communication or by use of financial mean, or otherwise, excites or attempts to excite, secession or armed rebellion or subversive activities, or encourages feelings of separatist activities or endangers sovereignty or unity and integrity of India; or indulges in or commits any such act shall be punished with imprisonment for life or with imprisonment which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine. Explanation.—Comments expressing disapprobation of the measures, or administrative or other action of the Government with a view to obtain their alteration by lawful means without exciting or attempting to excite the activities referred to in this section do not constitute an offence under this section.
results.answer:
Section 124A of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) defined sedition as any act by words (spoken or written), signs, visible representation or otherwise, that brings or attempts to bring into hatred or contempt, or excites or attempts to excite disaffection towards the government. The punishment was imprisonment up to seven years and a fine [IPC | repealed | substantive | Section 17].

Under the new Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), the specific section on sedition (Section 124A) has been deleted [BNS | active | substantive | Section 124]. Instead, Section 152 of the BNS criminalizes acts that purposely or knowingly excite or attempt to excite secession, armed rebellion, subversive activities, or separatist feelings, or endanger the sovereignty, unity, and integrity of India. The punishment is imprisonment for life or imprisonment up to seven years and fine. Comments on government measures to obtain change by lawful means are explicitly excluded from this offence [BNS | active | substantive | Section 152].

results.question: Did IPC have a provision for organised crime like the BNS section 111?
results.ground_truth: [IPC:] The IPC did not contain any standalone provision defining or punishing 'organised crime' as a distinct offence. Organised crime was addressed through special state enactments such as the Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act, 1999 (MCOCA) and central laws like UAPA and TADA (now repealed). General IPC provisions on criminal conspiracy (Section 120A-120B), dacoity (Section 391-400), and abetment applied to organised criminal activity but lacked the comprehensive syndicate-based framework. [BNS Section 111(1):] Any continuing unlawful activity including kidnapping, robbery, vehicle theft, extortion, land grabbing, contract killing, economic offence, cyber-crimes, trafficking of persons, drugs, weapons or illicit goods or services, human trafficking for prostitution or ransom, by any person or a group of persons acting in concert, singly or jointly, either as a member of an organised crime syndicate or on behalf of such syndicate, by use of violence, threat of violence, intimidation, coercion, or by any other unlawful means to obtain direct or indirect material benefit including a financial benefit, shall constitute organised crime. [BNS Section 111(2):] Whoever commits organised crime shall,—(i) if such offence has resulted in the death of any person, be punishable with death or imprisonment for life and shall also be liable to fine of not less than ten lakh rupees; (ii) in any other case, be punishable with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than five years but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine of not less than five lakh rupees.

results.question: Does IPC have community service as a punishment — and how is BNS different?
results.ground_truth: [IPC Section 53 — Punishments:] The punishments to which offenders are liable under the provisions of this Code are—First.—Death; Secondly.—Imprisonment for life; Thirdly.—[Omitted by Act 17 of 1949]; Fourthly.—Imprisonment, which is of two descriptions, namely:—(1) Rigorous, that is, with hard labour; (2) Simple; Fifthly.—Forfeiture of property; Sixthly.—Fine. [BNS Section 4 — Punishments:] The punishments to which offenders are liable under the provisions of this Sanhita are—(a) Death; (b) Imprisonment for life; (c) Imprisonment, which is of two descriptions, namely:—(1) Rigorous, that is, with hard labour; (2) Simple; (d) Forfeiture of property; (e) Fine; (f) Community Service. [IPC Section 53 contained no provision for community service. BNS Section 4(f) introduces community service as a new category of punishment for the first time in Indian criminal law.]
results.answer: No, the IPC (Indian Penal Code) does not mention community service as a form of punishment. In contrast, the BNS (Bharatiya Nyay Sanhita) explicitly includes community service as a possible punishment. For example, Section 209 of BNS states that failing to appear as required by a proclamation can be punished with imprisonment, fine, or community service, demonstrating that the BNS introduces community service as a penalty, which was not present in the IPC provisions listed.

results.question: What happens under IPC if a person under life sentence commits murder again — how does BNS differ on punishment?
results.ground_truth: 303. Punishment for murder by life-convict.--Whoever, being under sentence of imprisonment for life, commits murder, shall be punished with death. [BNS Section 104 provides:] 104. Whoever, being under sentence of imprisonment for life, commits murder, shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, which shall mean the remainder of that person's natural life.
results.answer:
Under the IPC, specifically Section 303 (now repealed), if a person who is already under a sentence of imprisonment for life commits murder again, the punishment prescribed is death [IPC | repealed | substantive | Section 303].

Under the BNS, Section 104 now governs this scenario. It provides that whoever, being under sentence of imprisonment for life, commits murder, shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, which shall mean the remainder of that person’s natural life [BNS | active | substantive | Section 104]. Thus, while the IPC mandated a death sentence, the BNS provides discretion to impose either death or life imprisonment for the remainder of the person's natural life.

results.question: What were the bail provisions in CrPC for non-bailable offences?
results.ground_truth: 437. When bail may be taken in case of non-bailable offence.—(1) When any person accused of, or suspected of, the commission of any non-bailable offence is arrested or detained without warrant by an officer in charge of a police station or appears or is brought before a Court other than the High Court or Court of session, he may be released on bail, but—(i) such person shall not be so released if there appear reasonable grounds for believing that he has been guilty of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life; (ii) such person shall not be so released if such offence is a cognizable offence and he had been previously convicted of an offence punishable with death, imprisonment for life or imprisonment for seven years or more.
results.answer: In the CrPC, bail for non-bailable offences could be granted when any person accused or suspected of such an offence was arrested or detained without warrant by an officer in charge of a police station or brought before a Court (other than the High Court or Court of Session). The person may be released on bail except: (i) if there were reasonable grounds for believing that the accused had been guilty of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life; (ii) if the offence was cognizable and the accused had previously been convicted of an offence punishable with death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for seven years or more [CrPC | repealed | procedural | Section 437].

results.question: Did CrPC allow video conferencing for producing the accused before a magistrate?
results.ground_truth: [CrPC Section 167:] The CrPC did not contain an explicit provision permitting production of the accused before a Magistrate via video conferencing or audio-video electronic means for purposes of extending remand. The accused was required to be physically produced before the Magistrate. (Some High Courts permitted video conferencing under inherent powers or under IT Act, but CrPC had no express provision.) [BNSS Section 187(4):] No Magistrate shall authorise detention of the accused in custody of the police under this section unless the accused is produced before him in person for the first time and subsequently every time till the accused remains in the custody of the police, but the Magistrate may extend further detention in judicial custody on production of the accused either in person or through the audio-video electronic means. [Key difference: BNSS expressly allows audio-video electronic production for judicial custody remand extensions (but not for the first appearance or for police custody extensions, which still require physical production).]
results.answer: Yes, as per the amendment by the State of Chhattisgarh, Section 251 of the CrPC allows for the accused to appear through the medium of electronic video linkage in the presence of his pleader in the Court [CrPC | repealed | procedural | Section 251].

results.question: What were the CrPC provisions for summary trials and have they changed in BNSS?
results.ground_truth: [CrPC Section 260(1):] Notwithstanding anything contained in this Code—(a) any Chief Judicial Magistrate; (b) any Metropolitan Magistrate; (c) any Magistrate of the first class specially empowered in this behalf by the High Court, may, if he thinks fit, try in a summary way all or any of the following offences:—(i) offences not punishable with death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for a term exceeding two years; (ii) theft, under section 379, section 380, or section 381 of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860), where the value of the property stolen does not exceed two thousand rupees; (iii) receiving or retaining stolen property, under section 411 of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860), where the value of the property does not exceed two thousand rupees... [BNSS Section 283(1):] ...shall try in a summary way all or any of the following offences:—(i) theft...where the value of the property stolen does not exceed twenty thousand rupees; (ii) receiving or retaining stolen property...where the value of the property does not exceed twenty thousand rupees. [Key difference: BNSS raised the monetary threshold for summary trial of property offences from two thousand rupees (CrPC) to twenty thousand rupees, reflecting inflation and enabling more cases to be disposed of summarily.]
results.answer:
Under the CrPC, provisions for summary trials were outlined in Section 262, which governed the procedure for summary trials. Additionally, Section 344 provided for a summary procedure for the trial for giving false evidence [CrPC | repealed | procedural | Section 262][CrPC | repealed | procedural | Section 344].

In the BNSS, the corresponding provisions are found in Section 285, which prescribes the procedure for summary trials and directs that the procedure specified for the trial of summons-cases shall generally be followed unless otherwise stated. BNSS also provides for summary procedure for trial for giving false evidence in Section 383 and contains a separate section (Section 286) dealing with the record in summary trials [BNSS | active | procedural | Section 285][BNSS | active | procedural | Section 286][BNSS | active | procedural | Section 383].

Therefore, while the essential framework for summary trials remains similar (with dedicated procedural sections and specific mention of summary trials for certain offences), BNSS introduces a more segmented structure by providing additional detailing in separate sections, such as the record-keeping requirement.

results.question: What was the old IEA rule about confessions made to police?
results.ground_truth: 25. Confession to police-officer not to be proved.—No confession made to a police-officer, shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence.
results.answer: Under the old Indian Evidence Act (IEA), any confession made to a police officer could not be proved as evidence against a person accused of an offence. This rule was clearly established in Section 25, which stated that confessions to police officers are inadmissible. Additionally, Section 26 further specified that no confession made while in the custody of a police officer could be proved against the accused unless it was made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate. However, Section 27 provided an exception, allowing information received from an accused in custody to be proved only so far as it distinctly relates to a fact discovered as a result of that information.

results.question: What was the IEA rule about statements made by people who are dead or unavailable as witnesses?
results.ground_truth: 32. Statements, written or verbal, of relevant facts made by a person who is dead, or who cannot be found, or who has become incapable of giving evidence, or whose attendance cannot be procured without an amount of delay or expense which, under the circumstances of the case, appears to the Court unreasonable, are themselves relevant facts in the following cases:—(1) When the statement is made by a person as to the cause of his death, or as to any of the circumstances of the transaction which resulted in his death, in cases in which the cause of that person's death comes into question. Such statements are relevant whether the person who made them was or was not, at the time when they were made, under expectation of death, and whatever may be the nature of the proceeding in which the cause of his death comes into question; (2) When the statement was made by such person in the ordinary course of business, and in particular when it consists of any entry or memorandum made by him in books kept in the ordinary course of business, or in the discharge of professional duty; or of an acknowledgement written or signed by him of the receipt of money, goods, securities or property of any kind; or of a document used in commerce written or signed by him; or of the date of a letter or other document usually dated, written or signed by him.
results.answer: Under the Indian Evidence Act (IEA), statements (written or verbal) of relevant facts made by a person who is dead, cannot be found, has become incapable of giving evidence, or whose attendance cannot be procured without unreasonable delay or expense, are themselves relevant facts in certain cases. Specifically, such statements are relevant when they relate to the cause of that person's death or to circumstances resulting in their death, in cases where the cause of death is in question. These statements are considered relevant regardless of whether the person was under expectation of death when making the statement or the nature of the proceeding in which the cause of death is questioned [IEA | repealed | evidentiary | Section 32].

results.question: Who has the burden of proof in a criminal case under the old IEA?
results.ground_truth: 101. Burden of proof.—Whoever desires any Court to give judgment as to any legal right or liability dependent on the existence of facts which he asserts, must prove that those facts exist. When a person is bound to prove the existence of any fact, it is said that the burden of proof lies on that person.
results.answer: Under the old Indian Evidence Act (IEA), the general rule is that the burden of proof in a suit or proceeding lies on that person who would fail if no evidence at all were given on either side. In criminal cases, when a person is accused of any offence, the burden of proving the existence of circumstances bringing the case within any of the General Exceptions in the Indian Penal Code or within any special exception or proviso, is upon the accused. Otherwise, the prosecution generally bears the initial burden to prove the case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt [IEA | repealed | evidentiary | Section 102][IEA | repealed | evidentiary | Section 105].

results.question: How did IEA Section 27 allow some police-obtained information to be used as evidence?
results.ground_truth: 27. How much of information received from accused may be proved.—Provided that, when any fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of information received from a person accused of any offence, in the custody of a police-officer, so much of such information, whether it amounts to a confession or not, as relates distinctly to the fact thereby discovered, may be proved.
results.answer: Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act allowed that when a fact is discovered as a consequence of information received from an accused person in police custody, only so much of that information as distinctly relates to the fact discovered may be proved in court. This means the law permitted as evidence only the part of the accused's statement that led directly to the discovery of new facts, regardless of whether it amounted to a confession or not [IEA | repealed | evidentiary | Section 27].

results.question: What was the IEA rule about expert opinions and how has BSA changed it?
results.ground_truth: [IEA Section 45:] Opinions of experts.—When the Court has to form an opinion upon a point of foreign law, or of science, or art, or as to identity of handwriting or finger impressions, the opinions upon that point of persons specially skilled in such foreign law, science or art, or in questions as to identity of handwriting or finger impressions are relevant facts. Such persons are called experts. [BSA Section 39:] (1) When the Court has to form an opinion upon a point of foreign law or of science or art, or any other field, or as to identity of handwriting or finger impressions, the opinions upon that point of persons specially skilled in such foreign law, science or art, or any other field, or in questions as to identity of handwriting or finger impressions are relevant facts and such persons are called experts. (2) When in a proceeding, the court has to form an opinion on any matter relating to any information transmitted or stored in any computer resource or any other electronic or digital form, the opinion of the Examiner of Electronic Evidence referred to in section 79A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (21 of 2000), is a relevant fact. Explanation.—For the purposes of this sub-section, an Examiner of Electronic Evidence shall be an expert. [Key differences: BSA adds 'any other field' broadening expert opinion beyond law/science/art; explicitly adds Examiners of Electronic Evidence as recognised experts for digital/computer evidence.]
results.answer:
Under the Indian Evidence Act (IEA), the rule about expert opinions was detailed in Section 45. It stated that when the Court had to form an opinion upon a point of foreign law, science, art, or as to the identity of handwriting or finger impressions, the opinions of persons specially skilled in those fields were relevant facts and such persons were called experts [IEA | repealed | evidentiary | Section 45]. Facts supporting or inconsistent with these expert opinions were also deemed relevant in Section 46 [IEA | repealed | evidentiary | Section 46].

The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) retains essentially the same position. Under Section 39 of BSA, expert opinions on points of foreign law, science, art, or the identity of handwriting or finger impressions remain relevant facts, and such persons continue to be called experts. The wording and scope remain largely unchanged [BSA | active | evidentiary | Section 39]. Section 40 of the BSA mirrors the principle that facts bearing upon expert opinions are also relevant, in line with what was contained in IEA Section 46 [BSA | active | evidentiary | Section 40].

In summary, the rule regarding the admissibility and relevance of expert opinions has been carried over from the IEA to the BSA without substantive change.

results.answer:
From the provided context of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), it appears that the law specifically addresses the admissibility and presumption of genuineness for electronic records. Section 63 states the admissibility of electronic records, while Section 81 prescribes that the Court shall presume the genuineness of certain electronic or digital records (such as those purporting to be Official Gazette or those directed by any law to be kept), provided they are kept in the form required by law and produced from proper custody. Section 93 further provides a presumption for electronic records that are five years old.

The inclusion of such explicit provisions for electronic records suggests that the BSA has adapted to developments in technology and evidence, potentially differing from older approaches where the Indian Evidence Act (IEA) may have treated documentary and oral evidence largely in the context of physical documents rather than digital/electronic forms. However, the specific differences in how the IEA previously handled electronic records as compared to the current approach under the BSA are not detailed in the provided context, so only the current BSA approach can be stated here.

results.answer: Under the Indian Evidence Act (IEA), a confession made by one person can be considered against other accused persons only when more than one person is being tried jointly for the same offence. results.question: Under IPC, was there a specific section on petty organised crime? What does BNS say?
results.ground_truth: [IPC:] The IPC contained no separate provision for 'petty organised crime.' Such activities were prosecuted under the general theft (Section 379), cheating (Section 420), or criminal conspiracy (Section 120B) provisions, without any enhanced punishment for the organised/gang dimension of minor offences. [BNS Section 112:] (1) Whoever, being a member of a group or gang, either singly or jointly, commits any act of theft, snatching, cheating, unauthorised selling of tickets, unauthorised betting or gambling, selling of public examination question papers or any other similar criminal act, is said to commit petty organised crime. Explanation.—For the purposes of this sub-section "theft" includes trick theft, theft from vehicle, dwelling house or business premises, cargo theft, pick pocketing, theft through card skimming, shoplifting and theft of Automated Teller Machine. (2) Whoever commits any petty organised crime shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than one year but which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
results.answer: Under the Indian Penal Code (IPC), there was no specific section that addressed 'petty organised crime.' However, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) introduces Section 112, which defines and covers 'petty organised crime.' According to BNS Section 112, any act such as theft, snatching, cheating, unauthorised selling of tickets, unauthorised betting or gambling, selling of public examination question papers, or any other similar criminal act committed by a member of a group or gang is considered petty organised crime. It provides an explanation that extends 'theft' to include trick theft, theft from vehicles, dwellings, businesses, shoplifting, pickpocketing, card skimming, cargo theft, and ATM theft [BNS | active | substantive | Section 112].

results.question: How does the new BNS deal with 'snatching' — was it a separate offence under IPC?
results.ground_truth: [IPC:] The IPC did not have a separate offence of snatching. Snatching was prosecuted as ordinary theft under IPC Section 378/379, or as robbery under Section 390/392 if force was used, without any distinct intermediate category. [BNS Section 304:] (1) Theft is snatching if, in order to commit theft, the offender suddenly or quickly or forcibly seizes or secures or grabs or takes away from any person or from his possession any movable property. (2) Whoever commits snatching, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine. [BNS thus creates snatching as a distinct named offence with its own punishment, sitting between ordinary theft (up to 3 years under BNS 305) and robbery (up to 10 years under BNS 309).]
results.answer: The new BNS (Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita) specifically and separately defines 'snatching' as an offence under Section 304. According to Section 304(1), snatching is described as theft wherein the offender suddenly, quickly, or forcibly seizes, secures, grabs, or takes away any movable property from any person or from his possession. Section 304(2) prescribes punishment for committing snatching, which may extend to three years of imprisonment and liability to fine [BNS | active | substantive | Section 304].

results.question: Can a person be convicted for conspiring or abetting a terrorist act even if no death results?
results.ground_truth: 113. results.answer: Yes, a person can be convicted for conspiring to commit or abetting the waging of war against the Government of India, which would include terrorist acts, even if no death results. Section 147 of the BNS makes it clear that a person who attempts to wage war, or abets the waging of such war, is punishable with death or imprisonment for life and is also liable to a fine. There is no requirement that death must result from the act of conspiracy or abetment for the conviction to occur. The provision covers the act of abetment itself, regardless of whether the ultimate consequence (such as death) actually occurs. Additionally, Section 48 establishes that a person can be held liable for abetment even if the abetment occurs outside India, as long as the offence is committed within India, reinforcing liability for abetment of serious crimes such as waging war or terrorism without the occurrence of death.

results.question: What does BSA say about oral evidence — must a witness testify directly about what they personally perceived?
results.ground_truth: 54. All facts, except the contents of documents or electronic records, may be proved by oral evidence. 55. Oral evidence must, in all cases whatever, be direct; that is to say—if it refers to a fact which could be seen, it must be the evidence of a witness who says he saw it; if it refers to a fact which could be heard, it must be the evidence of a witness who says he heard it; if it refers to a fact which could be perceived by any other sense or in any other manner, it must be the evidence of a witness who says he perceived it by that sense or in that manner; if it refers to an opinion or to the grounds on which that opinion is held, it must be the evidence of the person who holds that opinion on those grounds.
results.answer: According to Section 55 of the BSA, oral evidence must, in all cases, be direct. This means that a witness must testify directly about matters they personally perceived—oral evidence should be based on what the witness saw, heard, or otherwise experienced themselves, rather than through hearsay or indirect information.

Facts not otherwise relevant are relevant—(1) if they are inconsistent with any fact in issue or relevant fact; (2) if by themselves or in connection with other facts they make the existence or non-existence of any fact in issue or relevant fact highly probable or improbable.

results.question: Under CrPC, how was a judgment required to be pronounced in a criminal court — and what has BNSS changed?
results.ground_truth: [CrPC Section 353(1):] The judgment in every trial in any Criminal Court of original jurisdiction shall be pronounced in open Court by the presiding officer immediately after the termination of the trial or at some subsequent time of which notice shall be given to the parties or their advocates. [CrPC had no fixed time limit for pronouncement after the conclusion of trial.] [BNSS Section 392(1):] The judgment in every trial in any Criminal Court of original jurisdiction shall be pronounced in open Court by the presiding officer immediately after the termination of the trial or at some subsequent time not later than forty-five days of which notice shall be given to the parties or their advocates—(a) by delivering the whole of the judgment; or (b) by reading out the whole of the judgment; or (c) by reading out the operative part of the judgment and explaining the substance of the judgment in a language which is understood by the accused or his advocate. [Key difference: BNSS introduces a mandatory 45-day outer limit for pronouncing judgment after conclusion of trial; CrPC had no such time limit.]
results.answer:
Under the CrPC, the judgment in every trial in any Criminal Court of original jurisdiction was required to be pronounced in open Court by the presiding officer immediately after the termination of the trial or at some subsequent time of which notice was given to the parties or their pleaders. This could be done by delivering, reading, or reading and explaining the judgment as described in Section 353 [CrPC | repealed | procedural | Section 353].

For appeals, the rules in Chapter XXVII (which included Section 353) were made applicable to judgments in appeals by a Court of Session or Chief Judicial Magistrate, but unless otherwise directed, the accused was not required to be brought up to hear judgment delivered [CrPC | repealed | procedural | Section 387].

Under the BNSS, similar provisions apply: The rules in Chapter XXIX regarding judgment by a Criminal Court of original jurisdiction apply, in so far as practicable, to judgments in appeal by a Session Court or Chief Judicial Magistrate. The proviso remains that, unless the appellate court otherwise directs, the accused is not required to be present when the judgment is delivered [BNSS | active | procedural | Section 428].

Under the old CrPC (now repealed), Section 439 empowered the High Court or Court of Session to direct that any person accused of an offence and in custody be released on bail. The Court could also set aside or modify conditions imposed by a Magistrate when granting bail [CrPC | repealed | procedural | Section 439].

If the offence falls under sub-section (3) of section 480, it may impose any condition it finds necessary for the purposes mentioned therein [BNSS | active | procedural | Section 483].

results.question: Under CrPC, could a police officer discharge an arrested person without a magistrate order?
results.ground_truth: [CrPC Section 59:] No person who has been arrested by a police officer shall be discharged except on his own bond or on bail, or under the special order of a Magistrate. [BNSS Section 60:] No person who has been arrested by a police officer shall be discharged except on his bond, or bail bond, or under the special order of a Magistrate. [The substantive rule is the same in both CrPC and BNSS: a person arrested by police cannot be discharged without a bond, bail bond, or Magistrate's special order.]
results.answer: No, under the CrPC, a police officer cannot discharge an arrested person except on his own bond, on bail, or under the special order of a Magistrate. This means the discharge of an arrested person by a police officer requires one of these specific conditions and cannot be done arbitrarily or independently by the police officer without a magistrate's order in cases other than granting bail or bond.

results.question: How has the BNSS changed the rule about producing the accused before a magistrate compared to CrPC — is remote production allowed now?
results.ground_truth: [CrPC Section 167:] CrPC contained no express provision permitting production of the accused via video conferencing or audio-video means. The accused was required to be physically produced before the Magistrate for each remand (whether police custody or judicial custody). Some High Courts allowed video conferencing under inherent jurisdiction, but no explicit statutory authorization existed in CrPC. [BNSS Section 187(4):] No Magistrate shall authorise detention of the accused in custody of the police under this section unless the accused is produced before him in person for the first time and subsequently every time till the accused remains in the custody of the police, but the Magistrate may extend further detention in judicial custody on production of the accused either in person or through the audio-video electronic means. [Key change: BNSS expressly permits audio-video electronic production for judicial custody remand extensions. However, for the first appearance and all police custody remands, physical production before the Magistrate remains mandatory.]
